s: Chapter 9 personifies Wisdom, who builds her house with seven pillars, prepares meat and wine, sets her table, and sends out her maidens to call the simple and those void of understanding to eat her bread, leave their simple ways, and live. The chapter then gives teaching on how mockers and wicked people respond to correction compared with wise and righteous people, who grow in wisdom and learning. It states that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom and that being wise or mocking falls on the individual. In contrast, the foolish woman, loud, undisciplined, and ignorant, sits at her door in the high places of the city and calls the same simple passersby with the claim that stolen water is sweet. The chapter ends by warning that her guests do not know they are among the departed spirits in the depths of Sheol.

Wisdom builds her house with seven pillars, prepares meat and wine, sets her table, and sends out her maidens. She cries from the highest places of the city, inviting the simple to eat her bread and drink her wine, leave their simple ways, and live.

The foolish woman is described as loud, undisciplined, and knowing nothing. She sits at her door on a seat in the high places of the city and calls to passersby with the same invitation as Wisdom, saying stolen water is sweet and food eaten in secret is pleasant. Her guests are in the depths of Sheol.

The simple, described as void of understanding, are invited by Wisdom to turn in, eat and drink, leave their simple ways, and live. The foolish woman calls them with the same words, and the one who follows her does not know that her guests are the departed spirits in Sheol.
One who corrects a mocker invites insult, and the scoffer will hate someone who reproves him. The mocker who mocks alone will bear the consequence.
A wise person who is reproved will love the one reproving, and when instructed will become still wiser. The righteous person likewise increases in learning, and the wise person is wise for himself.

Wisdom's feast consists of prepared meat, mixed wine, a set table, and bread, offered to the simple and those void of understanding. Those who partake are urged to leave their simple ways, live, and walk in the way of understanding.

The fear of the LORD is called the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is understanding. Wisdom says that by her the days of her hearers will be multiplied and the years of their life increased.

Chapter 10 opens the proverbs of Solomon, a series of contrasting sayings about the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish. It contrasts diligence with laziness, honest and restrained speech with slander, violence and chatter, and shows the LORD blessing and protecting the righteous while the wicked lose hope, memory and a place in the land. Wealth and poverty are treated both as results of work and as sources of security or ruin. Love covers wrongs while hatred stirs strife, and the fear of the LORD prolongs life while the years of the wicked are shortened. Wisdom is shown in accepting correction and commandments and in careful, life-giving speech.

The LORD does not let the righteous go hungry, thrusts away the desire of the wicked, and brings blessing that adds no trouble. Fearing him prolongs days, and his way is a stronghold to the upright but a destruction to workers of iniquity.

l: upright and righteous people, Proverbs, Chapter 10
s: The righteous are blessed and remembered well, and righteousness delivers them from death. Their mouths are a spring of life, their labor leads to life, their desires are granted, and they stand firm forever and will never be removed.

The wicked gain nothing from their treasures, and their name will rot. What they fear overtakes them, their hope perishes, their years are shortened, and they will not dwell in the land. Violence covers their mouths, and their increase leads to sin.
Fools are portrayed as grieving their parents, chattering and falling, slandering, and dying for lack of understanding. Their mouths are near ruin, and they find pleasure in wickedness.
The wise in heart accept commandments, lay up knowledge, and restrain their lips. A wise son gladdens his father and gathers in summer, and a man of understanding finds pleasure in wisdom.

Righteousness is set against wickedness throughout the chapter: righteousness delivers from death, leads to life and brings blessing, while wickedness profits nothing, leads to sin and ends in perishing. Treasures of wickedness profit nothing, and the way of the LORD is a stronghold for the upright but destruction for those who do iniquity.

Speech marks character in this unit. The righteous mouth is a spring of life, choice silver and a source of wisdom that feeds many, while a perverse tongue is cut off. Hidden hatred, slander and many words bring harm, and restraining the lips is wise.

Wisdom is found on the lips of those with discernment and is produced by the mouth of the righteous. It shows in accepting commandments, heeding correction and laying up knowledge, while those void of understanding are met with the rod.

Chapter 11 is a series of proverbs contrasting the righteous with the wicked. It opens with the LORD's abomination of false balances and delight in accurate weights, and it sets humility and wisdom against pride and shame. The righteous are said to be guided by integrity, delivered from trouble and death, and repaid on earth, while the wicked are destroyed by their own perverseness, trapped by evil desires and left with hollow hopes. The chapter also covers the effect of each group on the city, warns against gossip, collateral for strangers and trust in riches, and contrasts those who scatter generously with those who withhold.
The LORD abominates a false balance and those perverse in heart, and he delights in accurate weights and in those whose ways are blameless.

l: the righteous and upright, Proverbs, Chapter 11
s: The righteous are guided by integrity and delivered from trouble and death, and their way is directed by their righteousness. Their blessing exalts the city, their desire is only good, and they flourish like a green leaf. Their offspring will be delivered, they bear a tree of life, and they will be repaid on the earth.

The wicked fall by their own wickedness and take the place of the righteous in trouble. When one dies, hope perishes, and his mouth destroys his neighbor and overthrows the city. They earn deceitful wages, expect only wrath, and will not go unpunished. The chapter says they will be repaid even more than the righteous.

Wisdom comes with humility, whereas pride brings shame. One who despises his neighbor lacks it, and a person of understanding holds his peace. A nation without wise guidance falls, but many counselors bring victory. He who is wise wins souls, and the foolish serve the wise of heart.

Righteousness delivers from death, directs a person's way and yields a sure reward and life, while wickedness brings death, treachery, trapping by evil desires and downfall. Those who seek good find favor, and evil comes to those who search for it. Riches do not profit in the day of wrath.

The one who scatters increases yet more, and the liberal soul is made fat, with the one who waters being watered in turn. The one who withholds more than is appropriate gains poverty. People curse someone who withholds grain, but blessing falls on the one who sells it. The merciful man does good to his own soul.

Chapter 12 is a series of contrasting proverbs about the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, and the diligent and the lazy. It says that those who love correction love knowledge, while those who hate reproof are stupid. It teaches that the righteous will be established, rescued, and kept from trouble, while the wicked are overthrown and filled with evil. It stresses the power of speech: lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, truthful words last forever, and the tongue of the wise heals. It also praises hard work, which brings bread and rule, and condemns laziness and chasing fantasies.
The LORD gives favor to a good man and condemns a man of wicked plans. He regards lying lips as an abomination, and those who do the truth are his delight.

The righteous have just thoughts, and their root shall not be moved and flourishes. Their house shall stand, and they come out of trouble. Their speech rescues them, and no mischief shall happen to them. A righteous man respects the life of his animal, and a righteous person is cautious in friendship. In the way of righteousness is life, with no death in its path.

The wicked give deceitful advice and speak words that lie in wait for blood. They are overthrown and are no more, and they are not established by wickedness. Their tender mercies are cruel, they desire the plunder of evil men, and they are filled with evil. Their way leads them astray.

The fool hates reproof and is called stupid. His way is right in his own eyes, and he shows his annoyance the same day. His heart proclaims foolishness. The one who chases fantasies is void of understanding.
The wise person listens to counsel, and his tongue heals. A man is commended according to his wisdom. The prudent man overlooks an insult and keeps his knowledge.

The diligent shall rule, while laziness ends in slave labor. Whoever tills his land shall have plenty of bread. The possessions of diligent men are prized, in contrast with the slothful man who does not roast his game.

Speech can destroy or heal. The wicked's words lie in wait for blood, while the speech of the upright rescues them. Rash words pierce like a sword, but the wise tongue heals. Truth's lips are established forever, a lying tongue is only momentary, and a kind word makes an anxious heart glad. A man is satisfied with good by the fruit of his mouth, but an evil man is trapped by the sinfulness of his lips.

Chapter 13 is a series of proverbs contrasting the wise, righteous, and diligent with scoffers, the wicked, fools, and the sluggard. It teaches that listening to instruction, rebuke, and correction brings honor, reward, and life, while refusing them brings poverty, shame, and ruin. It addresses the guarding of one's speech, the pursuit of desire and longing, and the nature of wealth, which is dwindling if gained dishonestly and growing if gathered steadily. It also observes that some pretend to be rich or poor, that companions shape a person's character, and that a father who loves his son disciplines him. The chapter closes by contrasting the satisfied righteous with the hungry wicked.
The wise son listens to his father's instruction, in contrast to the scoffer who ignores rebuke. A good man is also said to leave an inheritance to his children's children.
The scoffer does not listen to rebuke, in contrast to the wise son who heeds his father's instruction.

The righteous hate lies, are guarded by righteousness, and their light shines brightly. Prosperity rewards them, they eat to the satisfying of their soul, and the wealth of the sinner is stored up for them.

The wicked bring shame and disgrace, are overthrown by their own wickedness, and their lamp is snuffed out. Their bellies go hungry, misfortune pursues sinners, and a wicked messenger falls into trouble.
A fool exposes folly, and fools detest turning from evil. A companion of fools suffers harm.
The teaching of the wise is a spring of life that turns people from the snares of death. One who walks with wise men grows wise, and wisdom is found with people who take advice.

Whoever despises instruction pays for it, while one who respects a command is rewarded. Refusing discipline brings poverty and shame, heeding correction brings honor, and the one who loves his son is careful to discipline him.

Riches are the ransom of a man's life, yet some pretend to be rich while having nothing and others pretend to be poor while having great wealth. Wealth gained dishonestly dwindles, while wealth gathered by hand grows, and the sinner's wealth is stored for the righteous.

Chapter 14 contrasts the wise and the foolish, the upright and the wicked, through a series of proverbs. The wise build, think carefully, shun evil, and are slow to anger, while fools tear down, deceive, mock, and act recklessly. The upright fear the LORD and find a secure refuge, while the house of the wicked is overthrown. The chapter also addresses the treatment of the poor, saying that despising a neighbor is sin, while kindness to the needy honors their Maker. It closes with the claims that righteousness exalts a nation, sin disgraces a people, and the king favors a wise servant but is wrathful toward one who shames.

The LORD is feared by the one who walks in uprightness and despised by the perverse. The fear of him is described as a secure fortress, a refuge for children, and a fountain of life that turns people from the snares of death. He is also called the Maker of the poor, who is honored by kindness to the needy and held in contempt by those who oppress them.

The wise woman builds her house, and the wise man thinks about his way, fears and shuns evil, and is slow to anger. The lips of the wise protect them, the wise are crowned with riches, and wisdom rests in the heart of the discerning. The king favors a servant who deals wisely.

The fool tears down his house with his own hands, brings a rod to his back by his talk, and mocks atonement for sins. He is hot headed, reckless, and quick-tempered, and his folly is deceit. The text advises staying away from him because no knowledge is found on his lips.

l: upright and righteous people, Proverbs, Chapter 14
s: The upright walk in uprightness and fear the LORD, enjoy good will, and their tent will flourish. The evil bow down before the righteous, and in death the righteous has a refuge. Righteousness is said to exalt a nation.

The house of the wicked will be overthrown, and the wicked is brought down in his calamity. The wicked bow at the gates of the righteous, and those who plot evil go astray. The unfaithful will be repaid for his own ways, and sin is a disgrace to any people.

l: poor and needy people, Proverbs, Chapter 14
s: The poor person is shunned even by his neighbor while the rich have many friends. He who despises his neighbor sins, but he who has pity on the poor is blessed. Oppressing the poor shows contempt for their Maker, while kindness to the needy honors him.

Wisdom is built into the house, sought in vain by the scoffer but easy for the discerning, and it rests in the heart of those with understanding. Folly tears down the house, is inherited by the simple, and crowns fools with folly. The chapter sets the two against each other, as the prudent are crowned with knowledge and the quick-tempered display folly.

Chapter 15 of Proverbs contrasts the wise, the righteous, and the upright with fools, the wicked, and the proud through short sayings. It commends gentle answers, timely words, a cheerful heart, humility, and the fear of the LORD, while warning against harsh words, anger, greed, and scorning correction. The LORD is described as watching everywhere, detesting the sacrifices, ways, and thoughts of the wicked, delighting in the prayer of the upright, and hearing the righteous while being far from the wicked. Those who heed reproof are said to live and gain understanding, while those who refuse it despise their own souls and face death.

The LORD's eyes are everywhere, watching the evil and the good, and Sheol and Abaddon lie open before him. He finds the sacrifice, way, and thoughts of the wicked detestable, delights in the prayer of the upright, hears the righteous, uproots the house of the proud, and keeps the widow's borders intact.
The wise commend and spread knowledge, and a wise son makes his father glad. Their path of life leads upward, away from Sheol, and they seek counsel and keep their way straight.
Fools gush out and feed on folly, and their hearts do not spread knowledge. They despise a father's correction, and a foolish man despises his mother.

The wicked offer sacrifices and follow ways that are an abomination to the LORD, and their income brings trouble. Their mouths gush out evil, their thoughts are detested, and the LORD is far from them.
The house of the righteous holds much treasure, and their hearts weigh answers before speaking. The LORD hears their prayer, and the one who follows after righteousness is loved by him.
A gentle answer turns away wrath, in contrast to a harsh word that stirs up anger. A gentle tongue is called a tree of life, and a word spoken at the right time is called good and brings joy.

Reproof is heeded by the prudent and the wise, and the ear that listens to it lives and is at home among the wise. Those who hate or refuse it, such as scoffers and fools, face death, despise their own souls, and gain no understanding.

Chapter 16 is a collection of proverbs about the relationship between human planning and the LORD's sovereignty, the conduct of kings, and the contrast between wisdom and pride. The LORD is portrayed as weighing motives, directing steps, ordering all things for their end, and deciding the outcome of the lot. Kings are described as those whose throne rests on righteousness, who delight in truthful lips, and whose wrath or favor means death or life. The chapter praises getting wisdom and understanding above gold and silver, and warns that pride precedes destruction and a fall. It also describes the righteous, the wise, and the wicked through their speech and ways, ending with the claim that ruling one's spirit is better than taking a city.

The LORD gives the answer of the tongue, weighs motives, makes everything for its own end, and directs a man's steps. He abhors the proud, makes enemies peaceful toward the man whose ways please him, owns honest balances and scales, and decides every cast of the lot.

The king has inspired judgments on his lips, and it is an abomination for kings to do wrong because the throne is established by righteousness. Kings delight in righteous lips and value truth-speakers; the king's wrath is a messenger of death, while the light of his face is life and his favor like spring rain.

The wise man pacifies the king's wrath. The wise in heart are called prudent, their heart instructs their mouth and adds learning to their lips, and their pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones.

Getting wisdom is declared far better than gold, and getting understanding is better than silver. Understanding is called a fountain of life to its possessor, while fools are punished by their own folly.

Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD and will not go unpunished. Pride goes before destruction and an arrogant spirit before a fall, so it is better to be lowly among the poor than to share plunder with the proud.

l: the fear of the LORD, Proverbs, Chapter 16
s: Righteousness is valued above great revenues gained by injustice and is the foundation on which a king's throne is established. The highway of the upright is to depart from evil, and gray hair is a crown of glory attained by a life of righteousness.

Chapter 17 is a series of proverbs contrasting wise and foolish conduct, with attention to strife, justice, family, and speech. It states that quietness is better than a feast with strife, that the LORD tests hearts, and that those who justify the wicked or condemn the righteous are an abomination to him. It describes the fool as lacking understanding, grieving his parents, and unable to use money to buy wisdom, yet counted wise when silent. It praises the person of understanding, who responds to rebuke, spares words, and keeps an even temper, and it commends covering offenses, steady friendship, and a cheerful heart. It warns that wicked people take bribes, seek rebellion, and repay evil for good, and that strife should be stopped early like a breach in a dam.

The LORD tests hearts the way a refining pot tests silver and a furnace tests gold. He regards as an abomination both those who justify the wicked and those who condemn the righteous. Mocking the poor is said to reproach one's Maker.

The fool is shown as unable to profit from wisdom: money in his hand cannot buy it, a rebuke affects him less than a hundred lashes affect the wise, and his eyes wander to the ends of the earth. He brings grief and bitterness to his parents, and meeting him in his folly is called worse than meeting a bear robbed of her cubs. When he keeps silent he is counted wise.

The wicked person heeds wicked lips, receives bribes in secret to pervert justice, and seeks only rebellion, so a cruel messenger will be sent against him. One who repays evil for good will never see evil leave his house. Those with perverse hearts or deceitful tongues find no prosperity and fall into trouble.

The person of understanding is affected more deeply by a rebuke than a fool is by a hundred lashes, and wisdom is set before his face. He spares his words, is even tempered, and is thought discerning. A servant who deals wisely is said to rule over a shameful son and share the inheritance.

Strife is said to be worse than a feast, since a dry morsel with quietness is better than a feasting house full of it. Its beginning is likened to breaching a dam, so contention should be stopped before quarreling breaks out. Those who love disobedience love strife, and repeating a matter separates close friends.

Chapter 18 is a collection of proverbs contrasting the fool with the wise and the righteous, with a strong focus on the power of speech. It warns that the isolated man pursues selfishness and that a fool delights only in airing his own opinions, so his mouth brings strife, beatings, and destruction. It praises the LORD's name as a strong tower where the righteous find safety, in contrast with the rich man's imagined wall of wealth. It counsels humility, listening before answering, and seeking knowledge, and observes that the tongue holds the power of death and life. It closes on relationships: an offended brother is hard to win back, the poor plead while the rich answer harshly, and a true friend sticks closer than a brother.
The LORD's name is described as a strong tower to which the righteous run and are safe. A man who finds a wife is said to obtain favor from the LORD.

The fool takes no delight in understanding and wants only to reveal his own opinion. His lips bring strife and invite beatings, and his mouth is his destruction and a snare to his soul. Answering before hearing is called folly and shame.
The righteous run to the LORD's name, a strong tower, and are safe. This contrasts with the rich man, whose wealth is only an unscalable wall in his own imagination.

Speech is likened to deep waters, and death and life are said to be in the power of the tongue, with those who love it eating its fruit. A man's stomach is filled with the fruit of his mouth and he is satisfied with the harvest of his lips. The gossip's words are like dainty morsels that go deep into a person, while the fool's speech brings strife and ruin.
The fountain of wisdom is compared to a flowing brook. The ear of the wise seeks knowledge and the heart of the discerning gets it, and humility is said to come before honor.

Chapter 19 gathers proverbs contrasting the poor who walk in integrity with fools, liars, and the lazy. It warns that false witnesses will be punished and perish, and that wealth and gifts attract friends while the poor are shunned by relatives and friends. It praises those who gain wisdom, take counsel, restrain anger, and overlook offenses, and notes that the LORD's counsel prevails over human plans. It urges disciplining a son, warns against a son who robs his parents or ignores instruction, and describes the sluggard who will not feed himself. It closes by stating that penalties and beatings are prepared for scoffers and fools.

The LORD's counsel prevails over the many plans in a man's heart, and a prudent wife is said to be from him. Fear of the LORD leads to life and contentment, and he rewards whoever has pity on the poor, since that person lends to the LORD. A fool's heart rages against him.

The poor man who walks in integrity is called better than a perverse fool, and better than a liar. He is separated from his friend, shunned by all his relatives, and avoided by friends even when he pursues them with pleas. Whoever has pity on him lends to the LORD and will be rewarded.

The fool is described as perverse in speech, and his foolishness subverts his way while his heart rages against the LORD. Delicate living is not appropriate for him, and beatings are prepared for the backs of fools. A foolish son is called the calamity of his father.
The false witness is said twice not to go unpunished, and the one who utters lies will perish. A corrupt witness mocks justice, and the mouth of the wicked gulps down iniquity.

He who gets wisdom loves his own soul, and he who keeps understanding will find good. Listening to counsel and receiving instruction makes one wise in the latter end. A man's discretion makes him slow to anger, and rebuking one with understanding leads him to gain knowledge.
The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and will not even bring food to his mouth. Slothfulness casts one into deep sleep, and the idle soul will suffer hunger.

A foolish son is his father's calamity, and a son who robs his father and drives away his mother causes shame and reproach. A son is to be disciplined because there is hope, and he is warned that ceasing to listen to instruction leads him to stray from the words of knowledge.

Parents are told to discipline a son for there is hope, and not to be a willing party to his death. Penalties are prepared for scoffers and beatings for fools, and flogging a scoffer teaches the simple prudence. The hot-tempered man must pay the penalty, and rescuing him means doing it again.

Chapter 20 is a collection of proverbs contrasting wisdom and folly in everyday conduct. It warns against wine and beer, quarreling, laziness, gossip, rash vows, and cursing one's parents, and it praises integrity, counsel, and faithfulness. Kings are described as fearsome figures who judge, winnow out the wicked, and are kept safe by love and faithfulness. The LORD is said to detest differing weights and measures, to have made the hearing ear and seeing eye, to direct a man's steps, and to be the one to wait for rather than taking revenge. The chapter also notes that the human spirit is the LORD's lamp and that the sluggard who will not plow in winter will have nothing at harvest.

The LORD is said to detest differing weights and dishonest scales, and to have made both the hearing ear and the seeing eye. A man's steps are from him, people are told to wait for him to save them instead of repaying evil, and the spirit of man is called his lamp that searches the innermost parts.

The king's terror is likened to a lion's roar, and whoever provokes him forfeits his life. Sitting on the throne of judgment, he scatters evil with his eyes, and a wise king winnows out the wicked and drives the threshing wheel over them. Love and faithfulness keep him safe and sustain his throne.

The sluggard will not plow because of winter, so he begs at harvest and has nothing. A related warning says not to love sleep, lest poverty come, while opening one's eyes leads to being satisfied with bread.

l: differing weights and measures, Proverbs, Chapter 20
s: Differing weights and differing measures are called, both alike, an abomination to the LORD. The chapter repeats the point by saying the LORD detests differing weights and that dishonest scales are not pleasing.

A righteous man who walks in integrity is described as leaving blessed children after him. The chapter contrasts this with the many who claim unfailing love, asking who can find a faithful man, and with the buyer who calls goods no good and then boasts. It also condemns fraudulent food, dishonest scales, and differing weights and measures.

Chapter 21 is a series of proverbs contrasting the wicked with the righteous and the wise, and showing the LORD's sovereignty over human affairs. The LORD holds the king's heart, weighs the hearts of all, and prefers righteousness and justice to sacrifice. The wicked are shown as proud, violent, deceitful, and merciless, and they meet ruin, rejection of their sacrifices, and being ransoms for the righteous. The righteous and wise find joy in justice, life, honor, and treasure, while the sluggard, the pleasure-lover, and the contentious are warned against. The chapter ends by stating that no wisdom or counsel prevails against the LORD and that victory belongs to him, not to the prepared horse.

The LORD holds the king's heart in his hand like watercourses and turns it wherever he desires. He weighs the hearts of people, prefers righteousness and justice to sacrifice, and no wisdom, understanding, or counsel stands against him. Victory in battle belongs to him.

The wicked are described as proud, violent, devious, and desiring evil, showing no mercy to their neighbor. Their violence drives them away, their sacrifice is an abomination, and they are brought to ruin. The wicked serve as a ransom for the righteous, and a wicked man hardens his face.

The righteous find joy in doing justice and give without withholding. The Righteous One considers the house of the wicked and brings them to ruin. The righteous are ransomed by the wicked, and the upright establish their ways.

The wise receive knowledge when instructed and have precious treasure and oil in their dwelling, while a foolish man swallows such things up. A wise man scales the city of the mighty and brings down the strength of its confidence.

Doing righteousness and justice is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. It is joy to the righteous but destruction to workers of iniquity, and whoever follows righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.

Chapter 22 collects proverbs on reputation, wealth, and conduct. It values a good name over riches, notes that the LORD made both rich and poor, and warns that the rich rule the poor and the borrower serves the lender. It urges training a child in the right way, using discipline to drive out folly, and contrasts the prudent who avoid danger with the simple who suffer. The speaker then urges the reader to listen to the wise, claiming to have written thirty excellent things of counsel so that trust may be in the LORD. The chapter closes with commands not to exploit the poor, not to befriend the hot-tempered, not to co-sign debts, and not to move ancient boundary stones, and it praises the man skilled in his work who will serve kings.

The LORD is named as the maker of both rich and poor. His eyes watch over knowledge while he frustrates the words of the unfaithful. He will plead the case of the poor and plunder the life of those who plunder them, and those under his wrath fall into the adulteress's pit. The teaching is given so that the reader's trust may be in him.

The rich share with the poor the fact that the LORD made them all. They rule over the poor, and one who gives to the rich in order to increase his own wealth comes to poverty. Good name and loving favor are said to be better than riches.

The poor are made by the LORD just as the rich are, and they are ruled over by the rich. The text forbids exploiting them because they are poor or crushing them in court. The LORD will plead their case, and one who shares food with them is blessed, while one who oppresses them for gain comes to poverty.
A good name is declared more desirable than great riches, and loving favor is better than silver and gold. This opens the chapter as a value to be preferred over wealth.

l: child training and discipline, Proverbs, Chapter 22
s: The chapter says to train up a child in the way he should go, and when old he will not depart from it. It adds that folly is bound up in the heart of a child and the rod of discipline drives it far from him.

The reader is told to turn his ear, listen to the words of the wise, and apply his heart to the teaching. It is pleasant when kept within and ready on the lips. The speaker says he has written thirty excellent things of counsel and knowledge to teach truth and reliable words, so the reader can give sound answers to those who sent him.

Chapter 23 is a series of warnings and exhortations addressed to a son. It cautions him to be restrained when dining with a ruler, to avoid the food of a stingy host, and not to wear himself out chasing wealth that flies away like an eagle. It urges him to respect boundary stones and the fatherless, to accept discipline and correction, and to buy truth and wisdom. It calls on him to make his father and mother glad, and to avoid prostitutes and the wayward wife. It ends with a long warning against wine and drunkenness, describing the woe, poverty, confusion, and craving they bring.

The ruler is the host at a meal where the son is warned to consider carefully what is before him and not to desire his dainties, which are called deceitful food. Wealth and the ruler's table are treated as things not to crave.

The son is addressed throughout as the one being instructed. He is told to show restraint, apply his heart to instruction, accept correction, keep his heart on the right path, fear the LORD, avoid heavy drinking and gluttony, buy truth, and shun the prostitute and wayward wife. He is promised a future hope that will not be cut off, and is asked to give his heart to the speaker.

l: father and mother (of the son), Proverbs, Chapter 23
s: The son is told to listen to his father who gave him life and not to despise his mother when she is old. The father of the righteous and the parent of a wise child delight in him, and the father and mother are to be glad and rejoice. The speaker's own heart is also said to rejoice when the son speaks what is right.

Wine is presented as something not to be looked at when it is red, sparkling, and smooth going down. In the end it bites like a snake and poisons like a viper. Those who stay long at it or seek out mixed wine are the ones who suffer woe.

Wisdom, instruction, knowledge, discipline, and understanding are to be pursued: the son should apply his heart and ears to them, buy truth and not sell it, and accept correction, including the rod for a child, which is said to save his soul from Sheol. A wise heart brings gladness to the speaker and to the son's parents.

l: drunkenness and its effects, Proverbs, Chapter 23
s: Drunkenness and gluttony lead to poverty, with drowsiness clothing the drinker in rags. The drunkard is marked by woe, sorrow, strife, complaints, needless bruises, and bloodshot eyes. He sees strange things, imagines confusing things, and is like someone asleep in the middle of the sea. He is insensible to blows and wakes only to look for more drink.

Chapter 24 gathers proverbs urging the addressee, called 'my son', not to envy or join evil men, whose hearts plot violence, and instead to build life on wisdom, knowledge, and wise counsel. It calls for rescuing those led to death, warns that the one who weighs hearts will repay each person according to his work, and forbids gloating over an enemy's fall or taking revenge. The righteous man falls seven times and rises again, while the wicked are overthrown by calamity and their lamp is snuffed out. The son is told to fear the LORD and the king, to judge impartially, and to prepare his fields before building his house. The chapter ends with a narrator passing the sluggard's overgrown field and vineyard and learning that a little sleep brings poverty like a robber.

The LORD is warned of as the one who sees a man gloat over an enemy's fall, is displeased, and may turn his wrath away from the enemy. The text also calls him the one who weighs hearts, keeps the soul, and gives to every man according to his work. The son is told to fear the LORD and the king.

Wisdom is said to build a house, and with understanding and knowledge to fill its rooms with rare and beautiful treasure. A wise man has great power, and wise guidance with many advisors brings victory in war. It is too high for a fool, and is compared to honey that is sweet to the soul, bringing a reward and a hope that will not be cut off.

Evil men have hearts that plot violence and lips that talk mischief, and the son is told not to envy them or be with them. Those who plot evil are called schemers, and the wicked are overthrown by calamity, receive no reward, and have their lamp snuffed out. Whoever calls the wicked righteous will be cursed by peoples and abhorred by nations.

The righteous man is warned against by the wicked, who are told not to lie in wait against his habitation or destroy his resting place. The text says he falls seven times and rises up again, in contrast to the wicked, who are overthrown by calamity.

The son is addressed as 'my son' and told to eat honey, which stands for knowing wisdom, and to fear the LORD and the king. He is told not to envy evildoers, join rebels, show partiality in judgment, witness against his neighbor without cause, or take revenge. He is also told to rescue those led to death and to prepare his fields before building his house.

The sluggard is a man void of understanding, whose field and vineyard the narrator passes by. The narrator learns from this that a little sleep, slumber, and folding of the hands will bring poverty like a robber and want like an armed man.

l: sluggard's field and vineyard, Proverbs, Chapter 24
s: The sluggard's field and vineyard are seen to be completely overgrown with thorns, covered on the surface with nettles, with the stone wall broken down. The narrator considers this well and takes it as instruction about the consequences of idleness.

Chapter 25 opens with proverbs of Solomon that the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out. It contrasts God's glory in concealing a matter with the glory of kings in searching it out, and says the hearts of kings are unsearchable. It advises how to behave before the king, removing the wicked from his presence and not exalting oneself, and how to treat a neighbor: don't rush to court, don't betray confidences, and don't visit too often. It praises fitting words, wise reproof, faithful messengers, patience, and a soft tongue, while warning against boasting, false testimony, unreliable confidants, and singing to a heavy heart. It ends with kindness to a hungry or thirsty enemy, and images of restraint, such as not eating too much honey and a man without self-control being like a broken-down city.

Kings are said to find glory in searching out a matter, and their hearts are called unsearchable like the heavens and the earth. Their thrones are established in righteousness when the wicked are removed from their presence. They are to be approached humbly, since it is better to be invited up than put lower before the prince, and a ruler can be persuaded by patience.

The neighbor is someone to debate with directly rather than hastily taking to court, and whose confidence must not be betrayed, lest the betrayer be shamed and gain a lasting bad reputation. One should visit seldom to avoid wearying him into hatred, and false testimony against a neighbor is likened to a club, a sword, or a sharp arrow.

l: wise speech and conduct, Proverbs, Chapter 25
s: Fitly spoken words are like apples of gold in settings of silver, and a wise reproof is like a gold earring to an obedient ear. Faithful messengers refresh like cold snow at harvest, and patience and a soft tongue can persuade and break the bone. Restraint is urged, in eating honey, seeking honor, and governing one's spirit, along with kindness to an enemy who is hungry or thirsty, for which the LORD will reward.

Chapter 26 is a series of proverbs about fools, sluggards, and those who harm others with words. It opens with the fool, who is unfit for honor, needs a rod for his back, and is paired with contradictory advice about whether to answer him according to his folly. Honoring a fool, sending a message by him, or hiring him is compared to harmful or useless acts, and he repeats his folly like a dog returning to its vomit. The man wise in his own eyes is said to be less hopeful than a fool, and the sluggard is mocked for his excuses about a lion, his turning in bed like a door on hinges, and his laziness at the dish. The chapter ends with warnings about meddlers, deceivers who say they are joking, whisperers, contentious men who kindle strife, and malicious men who hide evil behind charming speech but will be exposed in the assembly and fall into their own pits.

The fool is said to be unfit for honor, to need a rod for his back, and to make a parable useless in his mouth. Advice is given both not to answer him according to his folly and to answer him so he is not wise in his own eyes. Honoring, hiring, or sending a message by him is likened to harmful acts, and he is compared to a dog returning to its vomit when he repeats his folly.

The sluggard makes excuses, claiming a fierce lion roams the road and streets. He turns on his bed like a door on its hinges and is too lazy to bring his hand from the dish to his mouth. He is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer with discretion.

l: man wise in his own eyes, Proverbs, Chapter 26
s: The man wise in his own eyes is mentioned in a rhetorical question. The text states there is more hope for a fool than for him.
The contentious man is compared to coals for hot embers and wood for fire, because he kindles strife. The text notes that a quarrel dies down without gossip, as a fire goes out for lack of wood.

The malicious man disguises himself with his lips while harboring evil in his heart. His charming speech should not be believed because seven abominations are in his heart. His malice may be concealed by deception, but his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly.

Folly is the basis for the contradictory instructions on answering a fool, either to avoid becoming like him or to keep him from being wise in his own eyes. The fool repeats his folly like a dog returning to its vomit.

Chapter 27 is a series of proverbs on boasting, praise, relationships, and prudent living. It warns against boasting about tomorrow and praising oneself, and says a fool's provocation is heavier than stone or sand. It values faithful friends, open rebuke, and a near neighbor over a distant brother, and notes that iron sharpens iron and that a contentious wife is like continual dripping. It also observes that Sheol and a man's eyes are never satisfied, that a fool cannot be cured of foolishness even when ground in a mortar, and that a man is refined by his praise. It closes by urging the reader to know the state of his flocks and herds, since riches do not last forever, and describes how they supply clothing, land, and food for the household and servant girls.
A fool's provocation is said to be heavier than a stone or sand. Even if ground in a mortar with a pestle along with grain, his foolishness would not be removed from him.

The wounds of a friend are called faithful, in contrast to the profuse kisses of an enemy. Earnest counsel from a friend brings joy like perfume and incense, and a man sharpens his friend's countenance as iron sharpens iron. The reader is told not to forsake his friend or his father's friend.

The reader is told to know well the state of his flocks and pay attention to his herds, because riches are not forever and the crown does not endure to all generations. The lambs provide clothing, the goats are the price of a field, and goats' milk feeds the family and the servant girls.

Chapter 28 contrasts the wicked and the righteous through a series of proverbs. The wicked flee without pursuit, lead lands into disorder, and fall into their own traps, while the righteous are bold as lions and are kept safe. Wicked rulers are likened to roaring lions and charging bears over helpless people, whereas rulers who hate ill-gotten gain have long days. Those who keep the law are called wise, and those who turn from it have even their prayers rejected. The chapter also weighs poverty against riches, valuing the poor person of integrity over the perverse rich, warning against hasty or oppressive pursuit of wealth, and promising no lack to those who give to the poor.

The wicked flee when no one pursues them, praise one another, and cause men to hide when they rise. Those who lead the upright astray fall into their own trap, those with perverse ways fall suddenly, and when the wicked perish the righteous thrive.
The righteous are as bold as a lion, contend with the wicked, and are kept safe when they walk blamelessly. When they triumph there is great glory, and when the wicked perish they thrive.

A poor person who walks in integrity is called better than a perverse rich one, and a poor person with understanding sees through the rich man. Oppression of the poor is condemned, and one who gives to the poor has no lack while one who closes his eyes to them will have many curses.
The rich man is described as wise in his own eyes, yet the discerning poor see through him. A rich person who is perverse in his ways is judged worse than a poor person of integrity.
A wicked ruler over helpless people is compared to a roaring lion or a charging bear. A tyrannical ruler is said to lack judgment, while one who hates ill-gotten gain will have long days.
Those who keep the law are wise and contend with the wicked, while those who forsake it praise the wicked. Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law has even his prayer called an abomination.

Wealth gained by excessive interest is gathered for one who pities the poor, and a person eager to be rich will not go unpunished. Working one's land brings abundant food, while chasing fantasies brings poverty, and the stingy man hurrying after riches does not know poverty awaits him.

Chapter 29 of Proverbs contrasts the righteous and the wicked, the wise man and the fool, and the effects of each on society. It warns that those who stiffen their necks against rebuke will be destroyed, and that people rejoice when the righteous thrive but groan when the wicked rule. It describes the duties of a king, who stabilizes the land by justice and fairly judging the poor but ruins it by taking bribes or listening to lies. It urges correcting children and servants, warns against anger, haste in speech, pride, and the fear of man, and says that those who trust the LORD are kept safe and that justice comes from the LORD.
The LORD gives sight to the eyes of both the poor man and the oppressor. Whoever trusts in the LORD is kept safe, and a man's justice comes from the LORD rather than from the ruler's favor.

The righteous thrive and cause the people to rejoice, and they can sing and be glad. They care about justice for the poor, will see the downfall of the wicked, and are detested by the dishonest, whom the upright in turn detest.

When the wicked rule the people groan, and when they increase sin increases. An evil man is snared by his sin, the wicked are unconcerned about knowledge, and the bloodthirsty hate the man of integrity and seek the life of the upright.
The fool vents all his anger, and in court against a wise man he rages or scoffs so that there is no peace. There is said to be more hope for a fool than for a man hasty in his words.
The wise man brings himself under control and turns away anger. Whoever loves wisdom brings joy to his father, and the wise man's dealings with a fool in court find no peace.

A king who rules by justice makes the land stable, while one who takes bribes tears it down. A king who fairly judges the poor will have his throne established forever, and a ruler who listens to lies has wicked officials. Many seek the ruler's favor, but justice comes from the LORD.

The righteous care about justice for the poor, and a king who judges the poor fairly will have his throne established. The poor man and the oppressor share this in common: the LORD gives sight to both.
The rod of correction gives wisdom, while a child left to himself shames his mother. A corrected son gives his parent peace and delight to the soul.

Those often rebuked who stiffen their necks are destroyed suddenly without remedy. The rod of correction gives wisdom and correcting a son brings peace, while a servant cannot be corrected by words alone, and pampering a servant from youth leads to a bad end.
Justice by the king makes the land stable, and the righteous care about justice for the poor. Though many seek the ruler's favor, a man's justice comes from the LORD.

Chapter 30 presents the words of Agur the son of Jakeh, who addresses Ithiel and Ucal, confessing his own ignorance and asking who has ascended to heaven and established the earth. He affirms that every word of God is flawless and warns against adding to it, then prays to be kept from falsehood and from both poverty and riches. He describes several wicked generations that curse parents, are self-righteous, haughty, or devour the poor. The chapter then lists numerical sayings about things never satisfied, things too amazing to understand, things that make the earth tremble, small but wise creatures, and stately marchers. It closes by urging restraint of foolish pride and noting that forcing wrath produces strife.

l: Agur the son of Jakeh, Proverbs, Chapter 30
s: Agur speaks to Ithiel and Ucal, declaring himself the most ignorant of men who lacks a man's understanding and has not learned wisdom. He asks who has ascended to heaven and established the earth's ends, affirms that God's words are flawless, and prays to be kept from falsehood, poverty and riches. He also delivers the chapter's numerical sayings and closing warning about wrath.

God is described as having every word flawless and as a shield to those who take refuge in him. He is the one implied to have ascended and descended, gathered the wind, bound the waters and established the ends of the earth, and people are warned not to add to his words lest he reprove them. He is also called the Holy One, the LORD, and the God whose name Agur does not want dishonored.

Agur asks God to give him neither poverty nor riches, but only the food he needs. He fears that fullness would lead him to deny God and ask who the LORD is, while poverty would lead him to steal and dishonor God's name.

l: generations of wicked people, Proverbs, Chapter 30
s: Four kinds of generation are described: one that curses its father and does not bless its mother, one pure in its own eyes yet unwashed from filthiness, one with lofty eyes and lifted eyelids, and one with teeth like swords and jaws like knives devouring the poor and needy. The eye that mocks a father and scorns a mother's obedience is said to be picked out by ravens and eaten by young eagles.

Three things that are never satisfied, and a fourth that never says 'Enough', are named: Sheol, the barren womb, the earth that is not satisfied with water, and fire. The leech is also said to have two daughters who cry 'Give, give.'

Agur says three things are too amazing for him, and four he does not understand: the way of an eagle in the air, of a serpent on a rock, of a ship in the middle of the sea, and of a man with a maiden. This is followed by the way of an adulterous woman, who eats, wipes her mouth, and claims to have done nothing wrong.

l: things the earth cannot bear, Proverbs, Chapter 30
s: The earth is said to tremble under three things, and not be able to bear four: a servant when he is king, a fool when filled with food, an unloved woman when she is married, and a servant who is heir to her mistress.

Four little creatures are called exceedingly wise: ants, which provide their food in summer; hyraxes, which make their houses in the rocks; locusts, which have no king yet advance in ranks; and a lizard, which can be caught by hand yet is found in kings' palaces.

Three things, and a fourth, are described as stately in their march: the lion, mightiest among animals, which turns away for none; the greyhound; the male goat; and the king against whom there is no rising up.

Chapter 31 opens with the words of King Lemuel, which his mother taught him as a revelation. She warns him not to give his strength to women or to drink wine and strong drink, lest he forget the law and pervert justice for the afflicted, and she urges him to speak for the mute and judge righteously for the poor and needy. The chapter then turns to a poem praising a worthy woman, who works eagerly with wool, flax, a field and vineyard, and merchandise, rises early to feed her household and servant girls, and gives generously to the poor. Her husband trusts her and is respected in the gates among the elders, and her children and husband praise her as excelling all other women. The chapter ends by declaring that charm and beauty are vain but a woman who fears the LORD shall be praised, and that her works should praise her in the gates.

King Lemuel is the son whom his mother addresses as son of her womb and of her vows, and the chapter presents her words as the revelation she taught him. He is told not to give his strength to women or to drink wine, and to open his mouth, judge righteously, and serve justice to the poor and needy.

King Lemuel's mother teaches him a revelation, addressing him tenderly as her son, the son of her womb and of her vows. She warns him against giving his strength to women and against kings' drinking, and charges him to speak for the mute and judge righteously for the poor and needy.

l: worthy woman (the woman of Proverbs 31), Proverbs, Chapter 31
s: The worthy woman is described as far more valuable than rubies. She works wool and flax, buys a field and plants a vineyard, rises at night to feed her household and servant girls, sells linen garments and sashes, opens her hands to the poor, and speaks with wisdom and kind instruction. She is clothed in strength and dignity, laughs at the time to come, and is praised by her children and husband, with the conclusion that a woman who fears the LORD shall be praised and her works should praise her in the gates.

l: husband (the worthy woman's husband), Proverbs, Chapter 31
s: The worthy woman's husband trusts her with his heart and will have no lack of gain, as she does him good and not harm all her days. He is respected in the gates when he sits among the elders of the land, and he praises her by saying many women do noble things but she excels them all.

l: the poor and needy, Proverbs, Chapter 31
s: In Lemuel's mother's instruction, the poor and needy are those for whom the king must open his mouth and serve justice, along with the mute and the desolate. The worthy woman opens her arms and extends her hands to them.
Justice is something kings risk perverting for the afflicted if they drink wine and forget the law. Lemuel is told to judge righteously and serve justice to the poor and needy.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: The LORD's word comes to Hosea son of Beeri during the reigns of kings of Judah and Israel, and tells him to take a wife of prostitution because the land commits great adultery by forsaking the LORD. Hosea takes Gomer daughter of Diblaim, who bears a son, a daughter, and another son. The LORD names the children Jezreel, Lo-Ruhamah, and Lo-Ammi, each name signaling judgment on the house of Israel, including the end of its kingdom and the withdrawal of mercy and relationship. The LORD promises mercy and salvation for Judah without weapons, and foretells that the children of Israel will become innumerable, be called sons of the living God, and be united with Judah under one head.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: The LORD speaks to Hosea, commanding him to take a wife of prostitution because the land forsakes him, and names each of the three children to signal judgment on Israel. He promises to avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu, to break Israel's bow, and to withdraw mercy from Israel, while having mercy on Judah and saving it without bow, sword, or horses. He also promises that Israel's children will be countless and be called sons of the living God, and that Judah and Israel will be gathered under one head.

l: Hosea, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Hosea the son of Beeri receives the LORD's word in the days of kings of Judah and of Jeroboam of Israel. He obeys the command to take a wife of prostitution, marrying Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and fathers a son, a daughter, and another son whom he names as the LORD directs.

l: Judah, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Judah's kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah mark the time of Hosea's word. The LORD says he will have mercy on the house of Judah and save it by the LORD their God, not by bow, sword, battle, horses, or horsemen. Its children will later be gathered with the children of Israel under one head.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Israel, under king Jeroboam son of Joash, is judged: the land commits great adultery by forsaking the LORD, its kingdom will cease, its bow will be broken in the valley of Jezreel, and it will receive no more mercy. Yet its children will become as countless as the sand of the sea, be called sons of the living God, and be gathered with Judah under one head.

l: Gomer, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Gomer the daughter of Diblaim is taken as wife by Hosea at the LORD's command. She bears a son, then a daughter, and after weaning the daughter bears another son.

l: Jezreel (Hosea's son), The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Gomer's first son is named Jezreel at the LORD's instruction. His name signals that the LORD will soon avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu, end the kingdom of Israel, and break Israel's bow in the valley of Jezreel. The text also says great will be the day of Jezreel.

l: Lo-Ruhamah, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Lo-Ruhamah is the daughter Gomer bears after Jezreel. The LORD has her named Lo-Ruhamah because he will no longer have mercy on the house of Israel. She is weaned before her brother is conceived.

l: Lo-Ammi, The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea / Chapter 1
s: Lo-Ammi is the son Gomer bears after weaning Lo-Ruhamah. His name means that Israel is not the LORD's people and the LORD will not be theirs. The LORD later promises that where it was said 'You are not my people,' they will be called 'sons of the living God.'

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: Chapter 2 presents the LORD speaking about a mother, who stands for the unfaithful people, and her children. The children are told to contend with their mother because she has played the prostitute, pursued her lovers, and credited them with the grain, wine, oil, wool and flax that the LORD actually gave, which were used for Baal. The LORD announces judgment: he will block her way, strip her, take back his gifts, end her feasts and Sabbaths, and lay waste her vines and fig trees. He then promises to allure her into the wilderness, speak tenderly, and turn the valley of Achor into a door of hope. He will make her call him 'my husband', remove the Baals' names from her mouth, establish peace, betroth her to himself forever, and show mercy to those who were 'not my people', who will answer 'You are My God!'

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The LORD declares he is no longer husband to the unfaithful mother and announces punishment: blocking her path with thorns and a wall, taking back his grain, wine, oil, wool and flax, and ending her feasts. He then promises to allure her into the wilderness, speak tenderly, break the bow and sword, betroth her forever, and have mercy on those who were not his people.

l: mother (Israel, the unfaithful wife), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The mother is accused of prostitution and of going after her lovers, whom she credited with her bread, water, wool, flax, oil and drink, not knowing the LORD gave them. She will chase her lovers without success, and be stripped and stripped of her gifts, then be allured into the wilderness, where she will respond as in her youth and be betrothed to the LORD forever.

l: children (Israel's children), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The children are told to say 'My people' and 'My loved one' to their brothers and sisters, and to contend with their mother. The LORD says he will have no mercy on them because they are children of unfaithfulness.

l: lovers (of the mother), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The lovers are the ones the mother follows, believing they give her food, drink, wool, flax and oil. She will not overtake them or find them, and her lewdness will be uncovered in their sight, with no one able to deliver her from the LORD's hand.

l: Baal, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The silver and gold the LORD multiplied for the mother were used for Baal, and she burned incense to the Baals in the days that the LORD will visit on her. The LORD promises to take the names of the Baals out of her mouth so they are no longer mentioned.

l: betrothal (of the LORD to his people), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The LORD promises to betroth the people to himself forever, in righteousness, justice, loving kindness, compassion and faithfulness, so that they shall know the LORD. In that day she will call him 'my husband' and not 'my master', and those who were 'not my people' will be called his people.

l: unfaithfulness and prostitution, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 2
s: The mother's prostitution and adulteries are the charge at the center of the chapter, and her children are called children of unfaithfulness. She is told to put them away from her face and from between her breasts, and the LORD's judgment, including stripping, wilderness and the loss of his gifts, answers them.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 3
s: The LORD commands the speaker to go again and love a woman who is loved by another and is an adulteress, as the LORD loves the children of Israel even though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins. The speaker buys her for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley. He tells her she must stay with him many days, not play the prostitute, and not be with any other man, and that he will be so toward her. The text then says the children of Israel will live many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod or idols. Afterward they will return, seek the LORD their God and David their king, and come with trembling to the LORD and his blessings in the last days.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 3
s: The LORD tells the speaker to go again and love a woman loved by another, an adulteress, as a picture of how the LORD loves the children of Israel even though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins. He is also called the God of the children of Israel, whom they will seek and come to with trembling, and whose blessings they will approach in the last days.

l: woman (loved by another, bought by the speaker), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 3
s: She is described as loved by another and an adulteress, and the speaker buys her for fifteen pieces of silver and a homer and a half of barley. He tells her she must stay with him many days, not play the prostitute, and not be with any other man, and that he will be so toward her.

l: children of Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 3
s: The children of Israel are loved by the LORD even though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins. They will live many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod or idols, and afterward will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king.

l: Israel's return to the LORD in the last days, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 3
s: Afterward the children of Israel are said to return and seek the LORD their God and David their king. They will come with trembling to the LORD and to his blessings in the last days, following the many days without king, prince, sacrifice, sacred stone, ephod or idols.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4 the LORD brings a charge against the children of Israel and the inhabitants of the land, declaring that there is no truth, goodness, or knowledge of God, only cursing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery, and bloodshed. Because of this the land mourns and its people, animals, birds, and fish waste away. The LORD rebukes the priests and prophet, saying his people are destroyed for lack of knowledge and that he will reject the priest who rejected knowledge and forgot God's law. The people consult wooden idols, sacrifice on hills under oaks, poplars, and terebinths, and indulge in prostitution and wine, which take away understanding. The LORD warns Judah not to follow Israel's offense, and says Ephraim is joined to idols and should be left alone, with the wind wrapping up the people and bringing disappointment over their sacrifices.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: The LORD brings a charge against the inhabitants of the land, saying there is no truth, goodness, or knowledge of God there. He declares he will reject the priest who rejected knowledge, forget the children of those who forgot his law, change their glory into shame, and punish and repay them for their ways. He warns Judah not to offend and says Ephraim should be left alone.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: Israel is called to hear the LORD's word and is described as having behaved extremely stubbornly, like a stubborn heifer. It plays the prostitute, and Ephraim is said to be joined to idols. Judah is warned not to follow Israel's offense or go to Gilgal and Beth Aven.

l: inhabitants of the land (Israel), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: The inhabitants are charged by the LORD with cursing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery, and bloodshed upon bloodshed. They are destroyed for lack of knowledge, eat without having enough, and practice prostitution and idolatry, so that they come to ruin without understanding.

l: land (Israel's land), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: The land will mourn because of the people's sins, and everyone who dwells in it will waste away. The animals of the field, the birds of the sky, and the fish of the sea will also die.

l: priests, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: The priests are accused of rejecting knowledge and forgetting God's law, so the LORD says he will reject them from being his priests and forget their children. They feed on the sin of the people and set their heart on iniquity, and the LORD says it will be like people, like priest, with punishment for both.

l: sins and moral corruption, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: The chapter lists cursing, lying, murder, stealing, adultery, breaking boundaries, bloodshed, prostitution, and drunkenness as the people's sins. These increased as the people multiplied, take away understanding, and bring the LORD's punishment, the land's mourning, and the people's ruin.

l: idols (wooden idol), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 4
s: The people consult their wooden idol and answer to a stick of wood, led astray by a spirit of prostitution. They sacrifice and burn incense on mountaintops and hills under shady trees, and Ephraim is said to be joined to idols.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 opens with the LORD addressing the priests, the house of Israel, and the house of the king, declaring judgment against them for being a snare at Mizpah and a net on Tabor. Ephraim and Israel are charged with prostitution and defilement, and their deeds and pride keep them from turning to God, so Israel, Ephraim, and Judah will stumble. Though they seek the LORD with flocks and herds, they will not find him because he has withdrawn. Alarms are sounded at Gibeah, Ramah, and Beth Aven, Ephraim is to become a desolation, and Judah's princes are accused of removing landmarks. Ephraim turns to Assyria and King Jareb for healing, but the LORD says they cannot cure him, and he will tear Ephraim and Judah like a lion and withdraw until they acknowledge their offense and earnestly seek him.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: Ephraim is known to the LORD and accused of playing the prostitute, being defiled, and pursuing idols. It stumbles in iniquity, is oppressed and crushed in judgment, and is to become a desolation. When it saw its sickness it went to Assyria and King Jareb, who cannot heal it, and the LORD will be like a moth and a lion to it.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: Israel is not hidden from the LORD and is defiled; its pride testifies to its face. Israel stumbles in its iniquity together with Ephraim and Judah, and the house of Israel is among those addressed in the judgment. Its tribes are told what will surely be.

l: Judah, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: Judah will stumble with Israel and Ephraim, and its princes are likened to those who remove a landmark. The LORD will pour out his wrath on them like water and be like rottenness to the house of Judah. Judah saw its wound, and the LORD will be like a young lion to it, tearing in pieces and carrying off with no one to deliver.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: The LORD speaks judgment against priests, Israel, and the king's house, saying he knows Ephraim and disciplines all the rebels. He withdraws himself so that those seeking him with flocks and herds cannot find him, and pours out wrath on Judah's princes. He will be like a lion, tear in pieces and go away, returning to his place until they acknowledge their offense and seek his face.

l: spirit of prostitution, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: The spirit of prostitution is said to be within the people, so that their deeds will not allow them to turn to their God. It accompanies their not knowing the LORD.

l: judgment, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 5
s: Judgment is declared against the priests, the house of Israel, and the house of the king, who have been a snare at Mizpah and a net on Tabor. Ephraim is crushed in judgment, and the day of rebuke will make it a desolation.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 opens with a call by speakers to return to the LORD, who has torn and injured them but will heal and bind their wounds, revive them after two days, and appear like the rain. The LORD then answers, asking Ephraim and Judah what He shall do with them, since their love is like a morning cloud and disappearing dew. He says He has cut them down through the prophets and the words of His mouth, and that He desires mercy and knowledge of God more than sacrifice and burnt offerings. He charges that they, like Adam, broke the covenant and were unfaithful, citing Gilead's iniquity and bloodstains, priests who murder on the path toward Shechem, and the prostitution and defilement of Ephraim and Israel. The chapter ends with a harvest appointed for Judah when the LORD restores the fortunes of His people.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: The LORD is described by the speakers as having torn and injured them yet as the one who will heal, bind wounds, revive them, and appear like the spring rain. He then asks Ephraim and Judah what He shall do with them, says He cut them down through the prophets and His words, and states that He desires mercy and knowledge of God over sacrifice. He accuses the people of breaking the covenant and sees a horrible thing in Israel, and He promises to restore the fortunes of His people.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: Ephraim is addressed by the LORD, who asks what He shall do to it because its love is like a morning cloud and early-vanishing dew. Ephraim is charged with prostitution, and with Israel it is described as defiled.

l: Judah, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: Judah is addressed alongside Ephraim, with the LORD asking what He shall do to it because its love is fleeting like a morning cloud and dew. It is also told that a harvest is appointed for it when the LORD restores the fortunes of His people.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: Israel is the house in which the LORD says He has seen a horrible thing. It is declared defiled, in connection with the prostitution found in Ephraim.

l: mercy and knowledge of God over sacrifice, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: The LORD states that He desires mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings. This is set against the people's fleeting love, their covenant-breaking like Adam, and the violence and shameful crimes described in Gilead and on the path toward Shechem.

l: return and restoration, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 6
s: The chapter begins with a call to return to the LORD, trusting that He will heal, bind wounds, revive on the third day, and come like the rain, and urging the people to press on to know Him. It ends with the LORD's statement that a harvest is appointed for Judah when He restores the fortunes of His people.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: Chapter 7 describes the LORD's desire to heal Israel being met by the exposed wickedness of Ephraim and Samaria, where falsehood, theft, and robbery prevail. The princes and king are portrayed as adulterers and schemers, burning like an oven with plots, drunkenness, and anger, and they devour their judges while their kings fall without anyone calling on the LORD. Ephraim mingles with the nations, loses strength without realizing it, and is likened to a pancake not turned over and to a dove easily deceived that calls to Egypt and goes to Assyria. The LORD declares he will spread his net over them, chastise them, and bring woe and destruction because they wandered from him, spoke lies against him, and plot evil despite his teaching and strengthening them. The chapter ends with their return not being to the Most High, their comparison to a faulty bow, and the prediction that their princes will fall by the sword and be derided in Egypt.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: Ephraim's iniquity is uncovered, and it is said to mix itself among the nations and to be like a pancake not turned over. Strangers devour its strength and gray hairs appear on it without its noticing, and it is likened to an easily deceived dove without understanding that calls to Egypt and goes to Assyria.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: Israel is the people the LORD would heal, but the exposure of Ephraim's and Samaria's wickedness prevents it. The pride of Israel testifies to its face, yet they have not returned to the LORD their God or sought him. They are compared to a faulty bow, and their princes will fall by the sword.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: The LORD wishes to heal Israel and says he remembers all their wickedness, which is before his face. He declares he will spread his net on them, chastise them, and pronounce woe and destruction on them for wandering from him and lying against him, though he would redeem them and had taught and strengthened their arms.

l: Egypt, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: Egypt is a place the easily deceived Ephraim calls to for help. It is also named as the land where the people's princes, having fallen by the sword for the rage of their tongue, will be held in derision.

l: Assyria, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: Assyria is named as a power Ephraim goes to, alongside calling to Egypt, like a dove without understanding. The LORD says he will spread his net on them when they go.

l: wickedness and falsehood of the people, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 7
s: The people commit falsehood, with thieves entering and robber gangs ravaging, and they gladden the king and princes with wickedness and lies. Their hearts burn like an oven with adultery, drunkenness, mockery, and smoldering anger, and they devour their judges. They do not cry to the LORD with their heart, plot evil against him, and speak lies against him, and their deeds have engulfed them.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 8
s: In Chapter 8 the LORD calls for a trumpet to sound the alarm because something like an eagle is over his house, since Israel has broken his covenant and rebelled against his law. Israel claims to acknowledge God yet has rejected what is good, set up kings and princes without the LORD's approval, and made idols from silver and gold. The LORD's anger burns against Samaria's calf idol, which a workman made and which will be broken in pieces. Israel sows the wind and will reap the whirlwind, is swallowed up among the nations, and Ephraim has hired lovers in Assyria. Ephraim's multiplied altars became places for sinning, the LORD's written law was treated as strange, and the LORD will remember their iniquity, punish them, and send fire on the cities of Israel and Judah after they forgot their Maker and built palaces and fortified cities.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 8
s: The LORD calls for the trumpet to be sounded because Israel has broken his covenant and rebelled against his law. He did not approve of their kings and princes, is angry at Samaria's calf idol, and does not accept their sacrifices. He will remember their iniquity, punish their sins, gather them, and send a fire on their cities.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 8
s: Israel claims to acknowledge God but has cast off what is good, and the enemy will pursue it. It set up kings and princes without the LORD's approval, made idols of silver and gold, and forgot its Maker while building palaces. It is swallowed up among the nations like a worthless thing, will return to Egypt, and will have fire sent on its cities.

l: Samaria, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 8
s: Samaria is told to throw out its calf idol, and the LORD's anger burns against them. Its calf is declared the work of a workman, not God, and will be broken in pieces.

l: molten images and idols (Ephraim's idols), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 8
s: The calf of Samaria was made by a workman and is declared to be no God. The LORD's anger burns against it, and it will be broken in pieces.

l: altars (Ephraim's altars), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 8
s: Ephraim multiplied altars for sinning, and these altars became for him altars for sinning. The LORD does not accept the sacrifices offered there, and he will remember and punish the iniquity.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 9
s: Chapter 9 warns Israel not to rejoice like the nations, because it has been unfaithful to its God and loves the wages of a prostitute at every threshing floor. The LORD announces that Israel will lose its harvests and its land, with Ephraim returning to Egypt and eating unclean food in Assyria, while Egypt and Memphis gather and bury the fugitives. The people will treat the prophet as a fool, though the prophet watches over Ephraim with God, and the text recalls their corruption at Gibeah and Baal Peor. Ephraim's glory is said to fly away like a bird, with no birth, no pregnancy and no conception, and the prophet asks the LORD to give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts. The LORD declares that he hated them in Gilgal, will drive them from his house, and will kill the beloved children of their wombs, so that they become wanderers among the nations.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 9
s: Israel is told not to rejoice like the nations because it was unfaithful to its God and loved a prostitute's wages at every threshing floor. It will lose its harvest and its land and will consider the prophet a fool because of its great sins and hostility. Its fathers were found like grapes in the wilderness but turned to Baal Peor and became abominable like what they loved.
